title: One coin at a time
translation: Nobody values a single moment. Is that because they understand it so well, or because they're fools? For the lazy fools, let me put it simply. A single coin weighs nothing, but pile enough of them up and a poor man becomes a rich one. That's why merchants care so much about every coin. You don't notice a moment, but if they keep on passing, the end of your life is there before you know it.
So if you're serious about the Buddha's way, don't worry about the months and years ahead. Worry about this moment, right now, going by for nothing.

Say someone came and told you that you were certain to die tomorrow. What would you count on until this evening? What would you do with the time? And how is today, the day we are actually living, any different?

Every day we lose a lot of time to things we can't avoid: eating and drinking, the toilet, sleep, talking, walking. In the little time that's left, we do useless things, say useless things and think useless things. And it's not just the hours. We use up days, we get through months, and that's how a whole life goes. Nothing is more foolish.

Xie Lingyun wrote down the Lotus Sutra as it was translated, but his mind was always on getting ahead in the world, so Huiyuan wouldn't let him into the White Lotus Society. Stop caring about the moment, even for a little while, and you might as well be dead.
So what is the point of valuing time? This: have nothing weighing on your mind and no business pulling at you. Then, if you mean to stop, stop. If you mean to practise, practise.

literal: There is no one who values an inch of time.
Is this because they know it well, or because they are foolish?
To speak for the sake of those who are foolish and lazy: though one coin is light, if one piles them up, it makes a poor person into a rich person.
So the merchant's care for a single coin is intense.
Though one does not notice an instant, if one carries them on without stopping, the time of ending one's life arrives at once.
So a person of the Way should not value the days and months far off, but should value the present single thought-moment passing in vain.
If someone came and told you that your life would surely be lost tomorrow, until today grows dark, what would you rely on, and what would you do?
The day of today in which we live: how is it different from that time?
Within one day, eating and drinking, relieving oneself, sleep, speech and walking cannot be avoided, and (we) lose much time.

In the remaining leisure, which is not much, to do useless things, say useless things and think useless things, and not only pass the time but use up days and pass through months and spend one's whole life: that is most foolish.
Xie Lingyun was the scribe of the Lotus (Sutra), but because his mind was always contemplating thoughts of wind and clouds, Huiyuan did not permit him to join the White Lotus fellowship.
When this is absent even for a while, one is the same as a dead person.
If you ask for what purpose one values time: it is that, with no cares within and no worldly affairs without, one who would stop should stop, and one who would practise should practise.

notes.text: {寸陰|すんいん}: 'an inch of shadow', the time it takes a shadow to move an inch, so a moment. It comes from a Chinese saying that every educated reader knew from the Thousand Character Classic: 'a foot of jade is no treasure; it is the inch of time you should fight for'.
{一銭|いつせん}: one coin, the smallest unit of money. Copper coins imported from China were in everyday use by Kenkō's time.
{道人|だうにん}: someone who follows the Buddhist way seriously, monk or not.
{一念|いちねん}: in Buddhist thought, a single moment of thought, the smallest unit of time. The instruction is to care about this one, not about the years.
A false friend: {便利|べんり} here means relieving yourself, going to the toilet, not modern 'convenient'. The list is the plain business of having a body.

notes.quote: 謝霊運は法華の筆受なりしかども
notes.text: Xie Lingyun (385–433), a Chinese poet and official, and a devout Buddhist. {筆受|ひつじゆ}: the scribe who wrote down a sutra as it was translated. Chinese sources link him with work on the Nirvana Sutra rather than the Lotus Sutra; Kenkō, or his source, names the Lotus.
'Thoughts of wind and clouds': ambition, the hope of rising in the world, as in the Chinese phrase {風雲|ふううん}の{志|こころざし}.

notes.quote: 恵遠白蓮の交はりをゆるさざりき
notes.text: Huiyuan (334–416) led a group of monks and laymen on Mount Lu who vowed together to be reborn in the Pure Land, later called the White Lotus Society. The story that he turned Xie Lingyun away because his mind was restless is told in later Buddhist collections. The 1925 edition writes 恵遠 for the usual 慧遠.

notes.quote: 止まむ人は止み、修せむ人は修せよ
notes.text: Commentators read this in different ways: stop doing wrong and practise what is good; or stop worldly business and practise the Buddhist way. Some connect it with {止観|しくわん}, a form of meditation ('stopping' the mind, then 'seeing'). The translation keeps it open.
